evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Model-Generated Clinical Summaries Through a Dual-Perspective Framework: Retrospective Observational Study
evidence.outcome: Differences between parent and clinician ratings of LLM-generated clinical summaries
evidence.effect: Parents and clinicians differed importantly on helpfulness; clinicians gave insight on clinical accuracy and parents on readability. No numeric results are reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: There were important discrepancies between parents and clinicians in the realm of helpfulness, along with important insights by clinicians assessing clinical accuracy and parents assessing readability.
evidence.sample_unit: pediatric cardiac intensive care unit notes

evidence.title: Improving patient understanding of oncology imaging: radiologist and patient evaluation of summarised versus full-length AI-simplified reports from a tertiary cancer centre
evidence.venue: Cancer imaging : the official publication of the International Cancer Imaging Society
evidence.outcome: Patient/public representative input in evaluating AI-simplified reports
evidence.effect: PPI readers (180 reads) preferred full-length version B (P<0.0001), differing from radiologist preferences in the lung cohort, showing that patient input revealed distinct preferences.
evidence.quote: While radiologists’ preferences differed between cohorts, with the lung cohort preferring the summary version and the colorectal cohort preferring the full-length version, patients’ overall preference was for the latter.
evidence.sample_unit: original CT oncology reports (30 colorectal, 30 lung), each simplified into two versions and rated by radiologists and PPI readers

commentary.bottom_line: Two offline rater studies found that parents and patient or public readers judged AI-generated text differently from clinicians, which suggests that including them in evaluation surfaces information clinicians alone may miss. No study measured whether this inclusion changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Two level 4 retrospective replay studies with raters test the practice, with 50 and 60 source documents. Both report that patient-side raters differed from clinicians. The design is offline, the outcomes are rater preferences rather than harms or benefits, and one abstract gives no numbers. Certainty is very low because of indirectness and imprecision.

In the pediatric study, clinicians contributed judgments on clinical accuracy while parents contributed judgments on readability. In the UK study, public readers preferred a different report version than radiologists did in the lung cohort. This suggests patient raters may catch comprehension problems that clinician review misses. No study tested whether patient raters catch errors that could reach patients.

PPI readers in the UK study completed 180 reads and preferred the full-length version B (P<0.0001), which differed from radiologist preferences in the lung cohort. This suggests structured patient rating can be added to an offline evaluation protocol. Neither study reports time, recruitment effort, or fidelity in a live pilot.

The HEAAL framework asks that fitness-for-purpose assessment engage patient community members from the target population. Neither study reports participant income, insurance, language, or literacy, so it is unknown whether the patient raters resembled the populations HEAAL is meant to protect.

The endorsements come from voluntary frameworks such as the CHAI guides and HEAAL, and from commentaries. The CHAI language ranges from should to may. None of the supplied sources cites a federal or state requirement to include patients in AI evaluation.

Parents in a pediatric cardiac intensive care setting rated helpfulness differently from clinicians, and UK public readers preferred a different report version than radiologists in the lung cohort. This suggests evaluations that exclude patients may approve outputs patients find less useful. The studies did not measure trust or access to a human.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared AI pilots conducted with and without patient or community participants on deployment decisions, detected errors, patient comprehension, or harm, and no study reports the staffing or cost of recruiting and compensating patient evaluators.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants, and the pediatric study did not report its country. Patient raters who were more literate or English-proficient than the target population may have missed readability problems that affect underserved patients most.
